  "insight": "The learner is struggling significantly with foundational concepts in both the introductory overview of data structures and the broader category of data structures algorithms, showing accuracies well below the competency threshold and a pattern of consistently choosing incorrect answer options.",

      "diagnosis": "Confusion between static and dynamic data structures; the learner repeatedly selects answer B when A is correct, indicating a misconception about mutability and memory allocation.",
      "next_steps": [
        "Review the lecture slide that defines static vs. dynamic structures; create a two‑column comparison chart with examples (e.g., arrays vs. linked lists).",
        "Watch the supplemental video on memory allocation for static and dynamic structures and take notes on key differences.",
        "Complete 10 targeted practice questions that explicitly ask for the definition or example of static vs. dynamic structures, then immediately check explanations.",
        "Explain the difference aloud to a peer or record a short video teaching the concept; this reinforces correct mental models."

    {
      "topic": "1.1 Introduction to Data Structures",

      "priority": "High",
      "diagnosis": "Pattern of over‑reliance on answer choice A or B without fully processing the question stem, leading to systematic mis‑selection.",
      "next_steps": [
        "Adopt a three‑step reading strategy: (1) underline the key term, (2) restate the question in your own words, (3) eliminate obviously wrong choices before selecting.",
        "Practice with a set of 15 “read‑and‑paraphrase” drills where you write a one‑sentence summary of each question before answering.",
        "Use a timer to ensure you spend at least 15 seconds analyzing each question before committing to an answer."
      ]

    {
      "topic": "Data Structures Algorithms",

      "diagnosis": "Misinterpretation of the primary purpose of data structures; the learner selects the most generic answer (A) instead of the nuanced answer (B) that emphasizes efficient data organization and algorithmic performance.",
      "next_steps": [
        "Re‑read the lecture notes section titled “Why Use Data Structures?” and highlight sentences that mention efficiency, organization, and algorithm support.",
        "Create flashcards that pair a data structure (e.g., stack, queue) with its core purpose; review daily until recall is automatic.",
        "Complete a worksheet that asks for the purpose of various structures in different scenarios, then compare your answers to the provided key."
      ]

      "topic": "Data Structures Algorithms",

      "next_steps": [
        "Implement a “choice‑verification” habit: after picking an answer, read the other options and justify why they are incorrect before finalizing.",
        "Do a short “answer‑justification” exercise: for each practice question, write a one‑sentence reason why the chosen answer is correct and why the others are not.",
        "Track your answer‑justification accuracy for the next 20 questions; aim for 90% correctness before moving on."
      ]

      "topic": "1.1 Introduction to Data Structures",

      "diagnosis": "Limited exposure to concrete examples; the learner appears to know definitions abstractly but cannot map them to real‑world data structures.",
      "next_steps": [
        "Build a simple cheat sheet listing each data structure covered (array, linked list, tree, etc.) with a real‑world analogy (e.g., array = spreadsheet row).",
        "Spend 15 minutes each day matching a definition to an example from the cheat sheet without looking at the labels.",
        "Use an online interactive visualizer (e.g., VisuAlgo) to see static vs. dynamic structures in action."
      ]

      "topic": "Data Structures Algorithms",

      "next_steps": [
        "Select two algorithms (e.g., binary search, breadth‑first traversal) and write a short paragraph describing why the chosen data structure is essential for its efficiency.",
        "Solve one algorithm‑design problem per day that explicitly requires choosing an appropriate data structure, then compare your solution to the model answer.",
        "Join a study group or forum thread where you explain your reasoning to peers; teaching reinforces conceptual links."
      ]
